tweets.text:
Normal, everyday people spent $759M using crypto cards in July.

I'm not talking about trading volume or onchain transfers. 9 million purchases at ~$86 each means it's more likely people buying groceries than whale activity.

You should pay attention because a year ago that number was only 306M.

When tracking started in late 2023 it was under $1M a month.

So this went from basically nothing to $759M a month in under 3 years.

Who's winning so far

The market already has clear leaders:
• @RedotPay → $395M in July (self-reported)
• @ether_fi → $100M
• @KASTxyz → $90M

Those 3 are 77% of everything tracked.

The giants are showing up

In crypto, the moment a product proves real demand, the giants move in. Basically crypto does the dirty work and then TradFi comes in when they smell blood.

And it's happening right now

• June 30: Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, Coinbase, BlackRock and Google, plus 140 other companies, announced their own stablecoin, $OUSD. Circle's stock dropped 16% that day.
• Visa turned on its own stablecoin platform in July.
• Mastercard is paying up to $1.8B for BVNK.
• Revolut already ships a card that spends crypto balances anywhere. Same product, and their users don't have to download anything.

What's interesting is over 90% of crypto card volume already runs on Visa's rails. The "disruptors" built their entire head start on Visa's network.

Visa collects a fee on every single one of those 9 million taps, and they can see this growth curve better than anyone.

The race that decides it

The way I think about this market now is a race with a head start. Crypto-native issuers got a 3 year jump and they're busy turning cards into a daily habit.

TradFi hasn't really entered yet, but when they do, the users are already sitting in their apps.

It's going to be hard for the crypto natives to out-distribute a bank.

The race that actually matters is whether crypto-native issuers can turn users into daily spenders faster than TradFi apps can turn on stablecoin rails.

Because once stablecoin cards feel normal, the winner is whoever makes the crypto part invisible.

It's interesting. We're finally reaching the end goal, normal people actually using crypto. 

It's just not as exciting as we imagined, because none of us degens are getting rich off a debit card chart.

𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪 𝗧𝗛𝗬𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗙

𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘵𝘰 𝘉𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘙𝘪𝘤𝘩 𝘞𝘪𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘉𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘓𝘶𝘤𝘬𝘺

Over the last 15 years, my portfolio is up 11,882%. Almost every major trade that got me there I discussed here on X, usually while taking it or a few days later, and explained why. No single investment contributed more than 10% of those returns. I consider myself lucky I never found one investment that made me rich. If you bought Bitcoin or a stock very early and it went up 100x, you may be rich, but that doesn’t prove you can repeat it. Early in my career I had several huge drawdowns, including quite a few around 50%. Today they are far fewer and smaller. Every mistake forced me to recalibrate. Over time, logic compounds.

A lot of you look at old traders as gods because they had one incredible period. One great call can make you famous for 20 years. But where is the repeatable track record? True legends are rare because their edge isn’t one trade or market. Their edge is how they think. Every time someone tells me, “Michael Burry said this,” my answer is: who cares?

At the entrance to the Temple of Apollo at Delphi were the words Know Thyself. Over the years I realized becoming a better investor was less about learning another industry and more about learning to see clearly. None of us sees base reality. We see it through years of opinions and filters. The less you color reality with opinions, the easier it becomes to see the facts.

I remember this with COVID. While the market acted like nothing serious was happening, I warned volatility was mispriced and recommended reducing risk. Before Russia invaded Ukraine, there was a massive military buildup while the U.S. was evacuating embassy personnel. I recommended buying $VIX. The same happened with Iran, I recommended buying oil before the escalation. In all three cases the information was public. People preferred opinions to reality.

$ZIM was another example. The market valued the company below its cash while it still held valuable assets and new ships coming. Shipping experts made fun of me because I was a generalist. They knew far more about shipping. But sometimes knowing every detail makes you miss the obvious. How can an analyst say a company should be worth roughly a quarter of its cash position while it still holds billions in valuable assets? Basic logic has to matter.

After enough years, your mind starts working almost like a probability machine. You collect the relevant variables, understand which matter, and they produce a range of outcomes. It is not always right. But when the facts are clear and price is far away from what they imply, you can make a lot of money. The trade idea I published on $INTC a few days ago is another example. With options, I don’t show every trade because people copy them without understanding risk management. That $INTC idea alone contributed roughly 7% to my portfolio this week and a half and will continue to compound this week. It is not always what you hold, but how you hold it.

Almost everyone publishing investment research has an incentive, and your benefit is usually not one of them. Think for yourself. If you bought Ethereum because Tom Lee, who makes around $10 million a year promoting Ethereum, told you to buy it without doing the work yourself, that is your fault, not his. You pressed the button. Blaming the person you followed teaches you nothing. Taking 100% responsibility does.

This is why I recommend a 10-day Vipassana retreat. Nothing will make you a better investor or human being than understanding how your mind works. For 10 days there is nowhere to run. No phone, no business, no entertainment. Just you and your mind. It is hard. That is the point.

Most people don’t lack information. They cover it with opinions. Reality does not care. See what is there. Understand the probabilities and risk-reward. Then act. Money was the byproduct. Becoming better was the real return. Know thyself. See clearly.

𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘵𝘰 𝘉𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘙𝘪𝘤𝘩 𝘞𝘪𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘉𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘓𝘶𝘤𝘬𝘺

Over the last 15 years, my portfolio is up 11,882%. Almost every major trade that got me there I discussed here on X, usually while taking it or a few days later, and explained why. No single investment contributed more than 10% of those returns. I consider myself lucky I never found one investment that made me rich. If you bought Bitcoin or a stock very early and it went up 100x, you may be rich, but that doesn’t prove you can repeat it. Early in my career I had several huge drawdowns, including quite a few around 50%. Today they are far fewer and smaller. Every mistake forced me to recalibrate. Over time, logic compounds.

A lot of you look at old traders as gods because they had one incredible period. One great call can make you famous for 20 years. But where is the repeatable track record? True legends are rare because their edge isn’t one trade or market. Their edge is how they think. Every time someone tells me, “Michael Burry said this,” my answer is: who cares?

At the entrance to the Temple of Apollo at Delphi were the words Know Thyself. Over the years I realized becoming a better investor was less about learning another industry and more about learning to see clearly. None of us sees base reality. We see it through years of opinions and filters. The less you color reality with opinions, the easier it becomes to see the facts.

I remember this with COVID. While the market acted like nothing serious was happening, I warned volatility was mispriced and recommended reducing risk. Before Russia invaded Ukraine, there was a massive military buildup while the U.S. was evacuating embassy personnel. I recommended buying $VIX. The same happened with Iran, I recommended buying oil before the escalation. In all three cases the information was public. People preferred opinions to reality.

$ZIM was another example. The market valued the company below its cash while it still held valuable assets and new ships coming. Shipping experts made fun of me because I was a generalist. They knew far more about shipping. But sometimes knowing every detail makes you miss the obvious. How can an analyst say a company should be worth roughly a quarter of its cash position while it still holds billions in valuable assets? Basic logic has to matter.

After enough years, your mind starts working almost like a probability machine. You collect the relevant variables, understand which matter, and they produce a range of outcomes. It is not always right. But when the facts are clear and price is far away from what they imply, you can make a lot of money. The trade idea I published on $INTC a few days ago is another example. With options, I don’t show every trade because people copy them without understanding risk management. That $INTC idea alone contributed roughly 7% to my portfolio this week and a half and will continue to compound this week. It is not always what you hold, but how you hold it.

Almost everyone publishing investment research has an incentive, and your benefit is usually not one of them. Think for yourself. If you bought Ethereum because Tom Lee, who makes around $10 million a year promoting Ethereum, told you to buy it without doing the work yourself, that is your fault, not his. You pressed the button. Blaming the person you followed teaches you nothing. Taking 100% responsibility does.

This is why I recommend a 10-day Vipassana retreat. Nothing will make you a better investor or human being than understanding how your mind works. For 10 days there is nowhere to run. No phone, no business, no entertainment. Just you and your mind. It is hard. That is the point.

Most people don’t lack information. They cover it with opinions. Reality does not care. See what is there. Understand the probabilities and risk-reward. Then act. Money was the byproduct. Becoming better was the real return. Know thyself. See clearly.

Open-weight models are rewriting AI economics

Open-weight AI models are quietly reshaping the economics of artificial intelligence. Here’s the simple breakdown:

Closed frontier models (the latest from OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) are proprietary. You can only access them through the company’s paid API. That gives those labs pricing power and very high inference margins. 

Open-weight models release the actual trained parameters publicly under permissive licenses (MIT, Apache etc.). Anyone can download them, run them on their own hardware, fine-tune them or host them. 

The strongest recent open models have come primarily from Chinese labs - DeepSeek (V4), Moonshot (Kimi K3), Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu/Z.ai (GLM 5.2), MiniMax and others; with important earlier contributions from Meta’s Llama series, Mistral and a few Western labs.

Why spend hundreds of millions training these models and then give the parameters (weights) away? 

1) Ecosystem power - Make your model the default foundation that developers, startups and companies build on.

2) Competitive pressure - High-quality free alternatives directly attack the high-margin API business of closed frontier labs.

3) Different business models - Many of these labs don’t need pure inference margins the way pure-play closed labs do. They monetise via cloud, enterprise services, hardware ecosystems, or parent-company funding.

4) Prestige - Talent attraction, and rapid community improvement.

Why are they so much cheaper? 

Once the weights are public, any cloud provider (or you yourself) can serve the model. Competition drives the price toward the actual cost of compute and electricity instead of a proprietary markup. Self-hosting removes the lab’s margin entirely. Many also use efficient architectures (especially sparse MoE designs).

Net effect:

- Dramatically lower barriers → faster AI proliferation across the economy.
- Higher intelligence-per-dollar for users.
- Structural pressure on the high inference margins of pure closed frontier labs.
- Value shifts toward infrastructure, efficient serving and the applications built on top.

Frontier closed models still win on the absolute hardest tasks and still capture most of the economic value today. However, open-weight models now handle a large and rapidly growing share of token volume (majority on several major platforms).
